title: Meta VR Glasses Launch at $1,299 With Muse AI, 5K Display and Hologram Calls
excerpt: Meta has unveiled $1,299 VR Glasses with a 5K micro-OLED display, eye and hand controls, and direct integration with its Muse AI agent.
author: The Quest for Profit

sources.name: Reuters — Meta unveils $1,299 VR glasses and expands Muse AI
Meta — Introducing Muse personal AI agent
Meta — Bringing private processing to Meta AI glasses

content: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has unveiled a new generation of virtual-reality hardware designed to shrink the traditional headset experience into a glasses-style device. Called Meta VR Glasses, the new product was presented at Meta Connect 2026 on September 23 and is priced at $1,299.99 in the United States. Meta says the device will go on sale in spring 2027 and weighs about 100 grams, roughly the weight of a deck of playing cards. The company is positioning the product not simply as a VR headset, but as a compact computing platform that combines immersive entertainment, gaming, productivity and artificial intelligence in a form intended to be worn for much longer periods.

The design represents a major departure from conventional VR hardware. Instead of placing the processor, battery and storage directly on the user's head, Meta has divided the system into two parts. The glasses contain the displays and sensors, while a separate puck connected by an optical tether handles computing, battery power and storage. According to Meta, this architecture is a major reason the device can weigh about 100 grams and remain substantially lighter than products such as the Meta Quest 3. The result is a pair of dark wraparound glasses rather than a large headset with straps and a bulky visor.

Meta is targeting high-end visual quality despite the smaller form factor. The glasses use what the company calls a 5K Infinite Display built from micro-OLED panels, delivering 37 pixels per degree. Meta says the compact pancake lenses were developed specifically for the glasses, while Dolby Vision support is designed to improve contrast and colour for compatible video. Dolby Atmos spatial audio is integrated into the frames, allowing the device to deliver immersive sound without requiring separate headphones.

The most important software feature is Meta's Muse AI agent, which Meta introduced earlier in September. Unlike a conventional voice assistant that primarily answers questions, Muse is designed to perform tasks on a user's behalf, including sending emails, booking travel, navigating websites and helping coordinate longer-term goals. Meta built Muse around a dedicated secure virtual machine and says users decide which services and apps the agent can access. At Connect, the company announced that Muse is being brought directly into its glasses, making the AI agent accessible while users are away from a phone or computer.

Meta's vision is for the glasses to make interaction with an AI assistant more natural. Users can talk directly to the device, while eye movements and hand gestures can be used to control functions such as launching applications, playing content and adjusting a virtual workspace. The system is designed to work without conventional controllers. That combination gives Meta another route toward its long-term goal of making AI a persistent interface that can follow users across devices rather than living exclusively inside a smartphone application.

The AI integration is particularly significant because Meta has been building Muse as a broader platform rather than a standalone chatbot. The company says Muse can continue working after a user closes the app and can return when a task needs approval or something changes. It can interact with websites, forms and selected services, and Meta has been adding payment and retail integrations. Bringing the same agent into glasses potentially gives users access to those capabilities through conversation and gestures while keeping their hands free.

Meta has also built privacy and security controls around Muse. The company says Muse runs inside a dedicated secure virtual machine, with another system called Sentinel monitoring actions and preventing internet access unless conditions are met. Sensitive credentials are stored separately, and users are asked for approval before actions such as sending email or making purchases. Meta says a future Confidential VM will encrypt the entire environment using a key held only by the user. These protections are particularly relevant when an AI agent is given access to personal accounts, shopping services and other sensitive information.

Entertainment is another major focus. Meta says the VR Glasses are the first IMAX Enhanced certified VR device and will support selected 3D films through Disney+ beginning in November in selected countries. The company is also working with numerous streaming and entertainment partners, including Prime Video, YouTube, DIRECTV, AMC+, Crunchyroll, Plex, ESPN and Tubi. Meta says thousands of titles could be available internationally by the time the glasses launch, with additional 3D content planned for 2027.

Sports are being positioned as another flagship use case. Meta says its immersive sports platform will provide front-row-style experiences with 180-degree viewing and 8K streaming for selected events. Once the glasses launch, the company says users could have access to more than 100 immersive live US sports events each year through partnerships involving organizations such as MLB, NBC Sports, TNT Sports and UFC. The proposition is intended to make a pair of lightweight glasses function as a private viewing screen rather than requiring a television or conventional VR headset.

Productivity is equally important to Meta's pitch. The glasses can create multiple virtual screens that appear around the user, allowing a large workspace to be generated almost anywhere. Meta says users can turn a flat surface into a virtual keyboard and touchpad, while full-colour passthrough allows them to continue seeing their physical surroundings. That could allow someone on a flight, in a café or at a desk to create a private multi-screen environment without carrying several monitors.

Gaming is another area Meta wants to expand. The company says more than 75 games will support hand-gesture controls at launch, while Xbox Cloud Gaming will provide access to hundreds of additional titles. The glasses are therefore being presented as a general-purpose entertainment computer capable of switching between movies, sports and games instead of being treated solely as a dedicated VR gaming product.

One of the more unusual announcements is Meta's hologram-calling technology. The company says VR Glasses can generate a photorealistic digital version of a caller, including real-time expressions and reactions, and place that person in the user's environment. Spatial audio is intended to make the person's voice appear to come from the holographic figure. Meta says the feature can work with common calling services including WhatsApp and Zoom, meaning people on ordinary phones or computers can still participate in a call and see the user's hologram on their screens.

The separate battery and compute puck helps solve one of the biggest problems in trying to make immersive hardware look like ordinary glasses: heat, power and weight. Meta says the puck provides up to three hours of continuous high-resolution media playback and supports 45W fast charging. Moving those components away from the face leaves the glasses themselves comparatively light, but it also introduces a cable connection and another physical object that the user must carry.

Meta is using Qualcomm's Snapdragon Reality Elite processor to power the system. The company says the chip enables high performance and fast load times while improving efficiency. Because much of the computing work is handled by the external puck, Meta can maintain the glasses-style design without attempting to fit a complete high-performance computer into the eyewear frame itself.

The launch places Meta in a competitive segment that has struggled to become mainstream. Reuters noted that Meta is targeting some of the capabilities associated with bulkier and more expensive devices such as Apple's Vision Pro, while trying to reduce the physical burden of wearing VR hardware. Market researcher Linda Sui told Reuters that the roughly 100-gram weight could improve the user experience, but also noted that the device's $1,299 price and familiar core use cases could make mass adoption challenging.

That price places Meta VR Glasses in a very different category from ordinary smart glasses. Meta's Ray-Ban products focus primarily on cameras, audio and AI interaction, while the new VR Glasses add immersive displays and spatial computing. The distinction is important because Meta is effectively pursuing two parallel hardware strategies: lightweight AI glasses designed for everyday wear and a more sophisticated VR device aimed at immersive computing.

The company is also expanding its AI-glasses range at the same time. Meta announced Ray-Ban Meta Audio, its first camera-free audio glasses, along with additional Ray-Ban and Oakley models. It says more than 100 AI-glasses styles across Ray-Ban, Oakley and Meta Glasses will be available by the end of 2026. The broader strategy is to make Meta AI available through increasingly different physical devices, with the glasses acting as a bridge between conventional smartphones and more persistent wearable computing.

Privacy remains a central issue for wearable AI, particularly because glasses can potentially observe and hear surrounding environments. Meta has responded by saying many simpler commands can be processed on-device and that more advanced AI workloads can use secure cloud infrastructure. The company argues that glasses have an advantage because they remain with the user throughout the day and can understand more context than a device that is frequently placed in a pocket.

The introduction of Muse to the glasses therefore changes the role Meta wants the hardware to play. The glasses are not simply a display mounted close to the eyes. They are intended to become a portal into an AI agent that can understand context, perform digital tasks and provide information without requiring the user to reach for a phone. In Meta's model, the glasses become a continuously accessible computing interface.

There are still practical limitations. Three hours of continuous high-resolution media playback is considerably shorter than the amount of time many users expect from conventional consumer electronics, although actual battery life will vary according to usage. The separate puck solves some weight and heat problems but introduces an external component and tether. The glasses also depend on a sophisticated software ecosystem and a growing library of immersive content to justify their premium price.

Whether consumers will embrace the format will ultimately depend on how naturally those capabilities fit into everyday life. Watching a movie privately on a plane, creating several virtual monitors in a café, controlling apps with gestures or asking Muse to perform a task are different use cases, but they all rely on the same premise: that a lightweight wearable can become a practical computer rather than simply an interesting VR accessory.

Meta's decision to announce the device alongside Muse is therefore strategically important. The company is no longer presenting VR as an isolated hardware business. It is connecting immersive displays, AI agents, spatial computing, entertainment, gaming and communication into a single platform. That approach could allow Meta to spread the cost of its hardware investments across several categories while giving users more reasons to stay within its software ecosystem.

For the VR industry, the device is also an experiment in form factor. Meta spent years developing conventional Quest headsets, but the new glasses show the company exploring what happens when the computer moves away from the face and into a small companion device. If the engineering works as intended, the technology could eventually enable even smaller glasses, longer battery life and more autonomous computing.

For now, Meta VR Glasses remain a future product rather than something consumers can buy today. The $1,299.99 device is scheduled to arrive in spring 2027, giving Meta several months to refine the hardware, expand its software ecosystem and build partnerships for immersive content.

The announcement nevertheless marks a significant step in Meta's hardware strategy. Zuckerberg is betting that the next major computing interface can move away from the phone and traditional VR headset toward something much closer to ordinary eyewear. By putting Muse directly into the operating system, Meta is also betting that AI agents will become the mechanism through which users interact with that new interface.
**What to Watch Next:**

The major milestones will be Meta VR Glasses' spring 2027 launch, independent testing of the 100-gram design, real-world battery performance and the quality of its 5K micro-OLED experience. Investors and consumers will also be watching how quickly Muse expands across Meta's glasses lineup and whether developers build useful applications around eye, voice and hand-based interaction.
